title: The Syllabus-First Era: When Disclosure Replaces Detection
content:
Hi [Name],

A governance shift surfaced across education communities this week that many principals will recognise — even if their policy PDF has not caught up.

State systems and major universities are converging on syllabus-first AI governance. Florida advanced rules requiring every course syllabus to disclose permitted student AI use and faculty AI involvement — with parent notification when instructional tools are approved. Oregon State, Duke, and Georgia Tech published parallel standards: human oversight on grading, faculty disclosure of their own AI use, and assignment-level permissions that override vague defaults.

The MIT AI report explained the student fracture behind the policy rush. Learners are not hiding AI — they are navigating contradictory rules course to course, with little justification. Office hours are thinning. Study groups are shrinking. Inconsistency is the crisis detection tools never solved.

Teacher and professor forums echoed the pivot. Surveillance stacks are losing credibility. Blanket bans feel dishonest. The emerging standard is a syllabus line — specific enough that parents can read it and students can cite it.

In India, NEET Round 1 counselling reignited the marks-versus-ranks debate. Over 11 lakh qualified, yet government MBBS allotment followed rank bands — including General-category seats beyond rank 20,000. Families hold scores that feel decisive until allocation logic tells a different story.

Phone-ban research added a sober note. Usage drops sharply under pouch policies, but year-one test scores remain near flat. Control without attention architecture is containment — not learning design.

Schools rebuilding credibility will publish a Syllabus-First Playbook: what is permitted per assignment, what proof is required, how parents are notified, and how faculty disclose their own AI use.
